title: After-action: surge observability gaps and targeted mitigation playbook for Dedicated pools
creator: Maya R. Thompson
description: Synthesis and action plan following a Dedicated capacity shortfall caused by an autoscaler regression during a traffic surge. Focuses on closing observability blind spots, adding protective controls, and concrete engineering tasks to prevent recurrence.
incident_summary: On 2025-03-10 a production surge from two customers exposed a regression in the Dedicated autoscaler. The autoscaler failed to provision sufficient warm capacity for heterogeneous instance types, leading to sustained queue growth, increased tail latency, and temporary throttling for several enterprise routes. Recovery required manual pool expansion and emergency traffic shaping.
detection: Alerts were triggered for per-pool queue depth and SLA breach after 7 minutes. Initial alerts showed high GPU memory pressure and backpressure on the fronting gateway. Existing metrics lacked a clear view of per-tenant admission rejections and warm-pool utilization by instance shape.
timeline: 2025-03-10 09:02 UTC - Traffic spike begins from two enterprise customers (billing sync + report generation).
2025-03-10 09:09 UTC - Queue depth alert for pool-dedicated-us-east-2 escalates; latency crosses 95th percentile SLO.
2025-03-10 09:12 UTC - Autoscaler logs show repeated failed scale-ups for A100-40G shapes due to transient placement throttling.
2025-03-10 09:20 UTC - Frontend gateway begins soft-throttling lower-tier customers to preserve quota for reserved pools.
2025-03-10 09:40 UTC - Engineering manually adds warm spare nodes and rebalances allocation; queue depth starts decreasing.
2025-03-10 10:05 UTC - SLOs return to nominal; incident declared resolved at 10:30 after verification.
2025-03-12 - Post-incident analysis meeting; identified gaps in autoscaler scoring and observability.
root_cause: A recent change to the autoscaler scoring weights (reduce weight on pending GPU capacity) combined with reduced warm-pool reserve for costly shapes caused the autoscaler to underprovision when placement latency increased. This was compounded by an observability gap: we did not track warm-pool hit rates per instance shape or per-tenant admission rejection counts, so detection and automated mitigation were delayed.
short_term_mitigations: Reverted the scoring weight change for the autoscaler (rollback commit abcd123).
Increased warm spare capacity for A100-40G and H100-80G pools by 15% for 72 hours.
Deployed a temporary upstream rate limiter to smooth bursts for non-enterprise tenants.
Added an emergency runbook step: automated warm-pool increase script to be triggered by queue-depth > threshold for >5 minutes.
long_term_remediations: Rewrite autoscaler scoring to include placement latency and per-shape warm-pool hit rate as first-class signals.
Implement per-tenant admission rejection metrics and expose them in Console as a top-level SLO dashboard.
Introduce a 'predictive warm-up' feature that uses short-term traffic forecasts and recent warm-hit rates to pre-warm shapes likely to be requested.
Add capacity chaos tests into CI that simulate placement throttles and verify autoscaler response within SLO windows.
Formalize burst-limiting policies in the routing layer with configurable tiers and soft/hard limits.

follow_up_measures: Weekly check-ins for first 8 weeks after release for warm-hit-rate and admission_rejection trends.
Post-deploy verification checklist added to PR template for any autoscaler-related change.
Customer outreach: notify affected customers with summary and compensatory credits offer for impacted requests.
runbook_changes: Add step: if queue_depth>X for >5min, trigger automated warm increase for affected shapes (script ID: scripts/warm_increase_v2).
Add step: temporarily divert non-enterprise routes when dedicated-pool SLO breach is detected and warm-pool increase fails.
Add post-incident checklist: collect autoscaler logs, placement traces, and warm-hit-rate time series and open a retro within 72 hours.
notes: This incident highlights a class of regressions where small tuning changes interact poorly with placement variability. Prioritizing observability and predictive warm-up will reduce blast radius for similar surges. Ensure product/solutions teams review burst policies for enterprise customers to align expectations.
